lang.name: Icelandic
lang.genderPrompt: Is this noun masculine, feminine or neuter?
lang.genderHelp: Every Icelandic noun is masculine (karlkyn), feminine (kvenkyn) or neuter (hvorugkyn). The gender decides which endings the word takes.
lang.pronNote: Icelandic spelling is close to its sound, but þ is "th" as in thin and ð is "th" as in this.

stages.title: The first 150 words
stages.why: The commonest 150 words are in almost every sentence. Learn these first.

stages.title: Words 151–400
stages.why: Now you can follow short, simple sentences about people, places and things.

stages.title: Words 401–750
stages.why: These words fill in everyday talk: time, family, work and food.

stages.title: Words 751–1,100
stages.why: Here the words get more specific, and the sentences get longer.

stages.title: Words 1,101–1,500
stages.why: These are less common words. Many appear in reading more than in speech.

ladder.title: Cases
ladder.intro: Icelandic nouns change their ending to show their job in the sentence. There are four cases: nominative (nefnifall), accusative (þolfall), dative (þágufall) and genitive (eignarfall). This ladder practises the endings, one noun at a time.

notes.title: Icelandic names
claims: Most Icelandic last names show the parent’s first name. They do not show a family line.
Unlike Denmark, Norway and Sweden, Iceland kept its traditional name system.
A last name is the parent’s first name in the genitive, then -son, “son”, or -dóttir, “daughter”.
If Jón Einarsson has a son named Ólafur, the son is Ólafur Jónsson.
Jón’s daughter Sigríður is Sigríður Jónsdóttir.
Since 1925, Icelanders cannot adopt a new family name unless they inherit the right to it.

notes.title: The Naming Committee
claims: The Icelandic Naming Committee keeps the official list of approved given names.
The committee was set up in 1991.
A name must fit Icelandic grammar, which gives every noun a gender and case forms.
A name may use only letters of the Icelandic alphabet.
Foreigners and their children may keep their own names.
In 2023, the register held about 4,300 names.

notes.title: The Christmas book flood
claims: The Jólabókaflóð, the “Christmas book flood”, is the yearly release of new books before Christmas.
People buy the books as presents to give on Christmas Eve.
Books are the most popular Christmas gift in Iceland.
A free catalogue called Bókatíðindi goes to every household.
Rules on imported paper were milder than on other goods, so books became the Christmas gift of choice.

notes.title: The sagas
claims: The sagas of Icelanders, the Íslendingasögur, are prose stories based on real events in Iceland.
The events took place in the ninth, tenth and early eleventh centuries, called the Saga Age.
They were written in Old Icelandic, a western dialect of Old Norse, mostly on calfskin.
They are the best-known examples of Icelandic literature.
Most were written down in the 13th and 14th centuries.
They focus on history, especially family history.
The people who wrote them down are largely unknown.

notes.title: Þorrablót
claims: Þorrablót is an Icelandic midwinter festival.
It is named for the month of Þorri, from mid-January to mid-February.
The word blót means “sacrifice”.
The modern festival began in the second half of the 19th century.
Icelandic students in Copenhagen held the first known celebration in 1873.
It is an evening with dinner, speeches and poems.
Today it can be a dinner with friends or a large event with stage shows and a dance.

notes.title: The settlement of Iceland
claims: The settlement of Iceland began in the second half of the ninth century.
Norse settlers crossed the North Atlantic.
Iceland was unsettled land, so people could claim it without fighting existing inhabitants.
Modern historians point to deeper reasons, such as a shortage of farmland in Scandinavia.
The Age of Settlement is traditionally said to have lasted from 874 to 930.
Íslendingabók and Landnámabók, from the 12th and 13th centuries, give much detail about the settlement.
These books are largely unreliable in their details.

notes.title: The Althing
claims: The Alþingi, or Althing, is Iceland’s national parliament.
It was founded in 930, and is called the oldest legislature in the world.
The word Alþingi means “general meeting”.
The first Althing met at Þingvellir, 45 kilometres east of where Reykjavík later became the capital.
After the union with Norway in 1262, it lost its power to make laws.
It got that power back in 1904, when Iceland gained home rule from Denmark.
Today it has 63 members, elected every four years.

notes.title: The change of religion
claims: Iceland became legally Christian in the year 1000.
The Althing voted to make Christianity the official religion.
The event is called the kristnitaka, “the taking of Christianity”.
Most early settlers were pagans who worshipped the Norse gods.
The two religions divided the country and threatened civil war.
The pagan law speaker Thorgeir Thorkelsson proposed “one law and one religion”.
Some compromises were given to the pagans in return for converting.

notes.title: The Cod Wars
claims: The Cod Wars were 20th-century confrontations between Iceland and the United Kingdom about fishing rights.
Each dispute ended with an Icelandic victory.
The confrontations came in 1958–1961, 1972–73 and 1975–76.
In 1958, Iceland expanded its territorial waters to 12 nautical miles.
A NATO-brokered agreement in 1976 ended the dispute. Britain accepted Iceland’s zones.
There was one confirmed death: an Icelandic engineer, in 1973.
Since 1982, a 200-nautical-mile zone has been the international standard.

notes.title: The Icelandic language
claims: About 390,000 people speak Icelandic, most of them in Iceland.
It is a West Scandinavian language, most closely related to Faroese.
It is not mutually understandable with Danish, Norwegian or Swedish.
It keeps a four-case grammar, which most other Germanic languages have lost.
The language authority coins new terms from older Icelandic words instead of taking in loanwords.
The oldest preserved Icelandic texts were written around 1100.
Icelandic Language Day is 16 November, the birthday of the poet Jónas Hallgrímsson.

notes.title: Icelandic letters
claims: The Icelandic alphabet has 32 letters.
It has no C, Q, W or Z, but adds Ð, Þ, Æ and Ö.
Six letters have acute accents: Á, É, Í, Ó, Ú and Ý.
The letters eth (ð), written dh, and thorn (þ), written th, are widely used.
Icelandic words never start with ð.
The letters æ and ö count as separate letters.
In 1973, Iceland replaced z with s in native words.

notes.title: Genders, cases and “the”
claims: Icelandic is a heavily inflected language.
Every noun is masculine, feminine or neuter.
Nouns change in four cases: nominative, accusative, dative and genitive.
Nouns also change for singular and plural.
Icelandic has no word for “a” or “an”.
The word for “the” is usually joined to the end of the noun.
Masculine nouns often end in -ur, -i, -ll or -nn.
This is not always reliable: Norður, “north”, is neuter although it ends in -ur.

notes.title: Icelandic sounds
claims: Icelandic has only very small differences in sound from region to region.
The main stress is always on the first syllable.
Icelandic stops differ by a puff of air (aspiration), not by voicing.
Preaspirated voiceless stops are common.
Length changes the meaning of consonants, but not of vowels.

notes.title: New words from old roots
claims: Linguistic purism is the policy of making new words from Old Icelandic roots instead of taking loanwords.
It began in the early 19th century, aimed at older loanwords, especially from Danish.
Today it targets English words.
The government supports it through institutions such as the Árni Magnússon Institute.
In the 16th century, Icelanders coined the word íslenska for their own language.
Eggert Ólafsson was the first real instigator of Icelandic purism.
